name: Yusuf Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, fine. I'm curious what you'll ask, to be honest. I've been reading about this stuff for a while.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a robot welding cell at a company that builds farm trailers. The robot does the long welds on the chassis, and I load the steel into the jig, the frame that holds it, start the program, watch the weld quality and touch up anything the robot misses by hand. When we change trailer models, I adjust the robot's path, and these days I use an AI assistant on my phone to help me work out the settings before I try them. Seven to four, with a half hour where everyone stands in the yard with coffee. I like the moment when a new program runs perfectly. I don't like the fumes, even with the extraction, or the paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you do anything outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a 3D printer in the garage and I make replacement parts for old motorbikes, knobs, clips, covers, that kind of thing. I sell them online, maybe 150 a month, more in spring. Hana says it's the only hobby she's seen that pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, it was overhyped, but the tools are still useful. I'd keep telling the lads at work to try the assistant for the welding settings, because it saves me a good half hour on a changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed. I'd hoped it would go further. But practically, nothing changes for us, and that's fine for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the job, keep using the AI for setups, keep growing the motorbike parts thing. Maybe buy a second printer, around 600, so I can keep up in spring. Keep saving as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a film that never got to the exciting part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your workmates think of you using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them think the assistant is cheating. Old Marek says if you need a phone to weld, you can't weld, and he's half right. But he still asks me to check his settings on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put more into the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more printers, if the side thing keeps growing. But I wouldn't leave the factory for it, the factory pays well and it's steady.

S0.say: It was overhyped, but the tools are still useful. I'd keep telling the lads to try the assistant for welding settings, because it saves me half an hour on a changeover.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped it would go further. But practically nothing changes, and that's fine for the mortgage.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for setups and grows his motorbike parts business, buying a second 3D printer for about 600. Keeps saving as normal.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a film that never got to the exciting part.
S0.quote: Old Marek says if you need a phone to weld, you can't weld, and he's half right.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf already uses AI daily and runs a small online side business, so even a plateau feels slightly flat to him. He's affectionate about sceptical colleagues like Marek and doesn't preach. The factory remains his anchor for steady pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you want to be the one who knows how the new stuff works. Learn it early, that's the advice I'd give anyone. And the company should pay for people to learn, that's just sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine, maybe better off. I already program the robot cell, so I'd be the obvious person to run two cells, or train others. The ones I'd worry about are the hand welders on the small batches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss straight away to put me on the robot manufacturer's programming course, the five-day one. I'd offer to train the others afterwards. And I'd use the AI to write up proper setup guides for each trailer model, so the knowledge isn't just in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, I'll admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it worry you that writing guides could make you easier to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. If I write down everything I know, the company needs me less, but if I don't, I'm the bottleneck and they'll replace me anyway. I'd rather be the one who wrote the guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek and the two hand welders. They're good, better than me with a torch. I'd tell the boss to keep them on the special orders, the custom trailers, because the robot's no good at one-offs.

S1.say: This is when you want to be the one who knows how the new stuff works, so learn it early. The company should pay for people to learn, that's just sense.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, maybe better off, since I already program the robot cell and could run two or train others. I'd worry about the hand welders on small batches.
S1.do: Asks his boss straight away for the robot maker's five-day programming course and offers to train others. Uses AI to write setup guides for each trailer model.
S1.quote: If I write down everything I know, the company needs me less, but if I don't, I'm the bottleneck and they'll replace me anyway.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf sees steady change as a promotion path and moves first. He thinks hard about the trade-off of writing down his know-how and chooses openness. He looks out for the skilled hand welders, suggesting a practical role for them on one-offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, and the sensible thing is to work out quickly how people keep an income while it settles. Government and companies both need to move faster than they've ever moved. Arguing about who's to blame won't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if AI can do anything, it can program a welding robot better than me. My edge is gone within a year. I'd be one of the last out, maybe, but out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the factory as long as I'm useful, running the changeover. At the same time I'd put about 8,000 of savings into a small robot arm and a better printer for the garage, to make parts on a bigger scale. If robots are going to do the work, I'd rather own one. And we'd cut back at home, no holiday, until we see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and scared together, which is a strange mix at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the motorbike parts business survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if people still have money. That's the thing I don't know. If everyone's out of work, nobody's restoring old motorbikes. So it's a gamble, but a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does two years of warning help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough to set something up, not enough to see if it works before everything changes. With two years I'd be building the boat while the water's already coming in.

S2.say: It's here, so we need to work out quickly how people keep an income while it settles. Government and companies need to move faster than ever, and arguing about blame won't help.
S2.think: If AI can do anything, it can program a welding robot better than me, so my edge is gone within a year. I'd be one of the last out, but out.
S2.do: Stays to run the changeover at the factory while putting about 8,000 of savings into a small robot arm and a better printer for the garage business. Cuts back at home and skips the holiday.
S2.feel: Anxious, with excitement and fear mixed together in the middle of the night.
S2.quote: With two years I'd be building the boat while the water's already coming in.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf's answer to fast AGI is to own a robot rather than compete with one. He's clear-eyed that his side business depends on other people still having money. The mix of excitement and fear is honest and fits his adaptable, pragmatic temperament.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning. Use it. Train people, set up some kind of income support, and let companies change at a pace that doesn't wreck towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is enough time to build the side business properly. Three or four years of the factory paying the mortgage, while the garage grows into something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the robot programming course, get as much as I can from the factory, and grow the parts business to maybe 500 a month. By year three I'd rent a small unit on the industrial estate and buy a robot arm for finishing. I'd keep at least six months of savings untouched the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I feel like I'd have the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana's careful. She'd want me to keep the factory job until the business makes as much as my wage. She'd say a hobby that pays for itself isn't the same as a job that pays for the house. She's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years feel compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm grabbing at it. With five I can test it, fail a bit, fix it. That's how I like to work, actually, small steps you can check.

S3.say: Five years is a fair warning, so use it: train people, set up income support and let companies change at a pace that doesn't wreck towns.
S3.think: This is enough time to build the side business properly. The factory pays the mortgage for three or four years while the garage grows into something real.
S3.do: Takes the robot programming course and grows the parts business towards 500 a month in the first year. Rents a small unit and buys a finishing robot arm by year three, keeping six months of savings untouched.
S3.quote: She'd say a hobby that pays for itself isn't the same as a job that pays for the house.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Yusuf work the way he likes, in small checkable steps. His wife's caution acts as a brake he respects. The plan is concrete, with numbers, dates and a fallback cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, if we use it. Get young people learning the right things, help older workers move, and don't pretend it's not coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd come out of this fine. Ten years is enough to have the business running on its own, the mortgage mostly paid, and the kids through school. I'd be fifty-three and doing something I chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the factory for five or six years, learning everything about the new robots as they come in. Meanwhile I'd grow the parts business step by step and move it into a unit around year five. I'd put a bit into an index fund every month too, a couple of hundred, so we're not betting everything on one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit nervous about the end, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the kids get involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emil already helps with the printer. I'd want him to know how to make things, not just how to ask a machine to make them. Zofia's into drawing, so maybe she'd do the designs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody has money to buy anything at the end. That's not something I can fix from my garage. That one's for the people in charge.

S4.say: Ten years is a real chance if we use it: get young people learning the right things, help older workers move and don't pretend it's not coming.
S4.think: I think we'd come out fine, with the business running on its own, the mortgage mostly paid and the kids through school. At fifty-three I'd be doing something I chose.
S4.do: Stays at the factory for five or six years learning the new robots while growing the parts business, moving it to a unit around year five. Puts a couple of hundred a month into an index fund to spread the risk.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a bit nervous about the end.
S4.quote: I'd want him to know how to make things, not just how to ask a machine to make them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Yusuf is genuinely calm and sees the change working in his favour. His remaining worry is whether anyone will have money to spend, which he sees as beyond his control. The family-business picture with his children is a hopeful touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I couldn't test anything before it all moved. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses to buy their own robots, and some income support so people have money to spend. Without customers, all the robots in the world don't help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if the robots will take our jobs, nobody asks whose robots they'll be. That's the question I'd want answered.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots will take our jobs, nobody asks whose robots they'll be.
portrait: Yusuf Kowalski is 43, runs a robot welding cell at a farm-trailer maker, and sells 3D-printed motorbike parts from his garage on the side. He's curious, pragmatic and uses AI every day, married to Hana, a careful partner who keeps him grounded, with two children. He's calm through a plateau and steady change, seeing himself as the one who learns first. Two-year AGI makes him anxious and he responds by buying his own robot arm, while five and ten years let him grow the side business step by step, ending mostly calm but worried about whether customers will still have money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he couldn't test anything before everything moved.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses to buy their own robots and income support so people still have money to spend.
